articles.title_original: Dual-doped all-graphene fiber for flexible, high-performance thermoelectric temperature sensing
articles.title_en: Dual-doped graphene fiber enables flexible high-performance temperature sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract High-performance temperature sensors are critical components for emerging Internet-of-Things and biomedical-electronics platforms. However, simultaneously achieving high sensitivity, mechanical compliance, and user-defined integrability remains a formidable materials-and-device challenge. Here, we report a continuous graphene fiber (GF) thermocouple technology where multiple p–n thermocouples are created in situ along a single, unbroken fiber while preserving its structural integrity. By periodically modulating surface charge-transfer doping with polyethyleneimine (PEI) and FeCl 3 , we formed an array of ten p–n pairs that delivered an exceptional thermocouple sensitivity of 452.32 µV K −1 . The device retained ~97.8% of its initial sensitivity after 10,000 bending cycles at a 5-mm radius, confirming robustness under repeated mechanical deformation. When deployed on skin, the sensor tracked dynamic body temperature variations with a measurement error of 0.64%, validating its practical value for real-time, non-invasive health monitoring. These results establish all-carbon GF thermocouples as a high-precision and mechanically adaptable temperature-sensing platform for next-generation wearable electronics and personalized healthcare systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a continuous graphene-fiber thermocouple with in-fiber p–n pairs formed through periodic PEI and FeCl₃ doping. The sensor achieved 452.32 µV K⁻¹ sensitivity, retained about 97.8% performance after 10,000 bends, and measured skin temperature with 0.64% error, indicating potential for wearable and biomedical monitoring.

articles.title_original: Visualizing flat-band spatial renormalization in rhombohedral graphene superlattices
articles.title_en: STM Visualizes Flat-Band Renormalization in Rhombohedral Graphene Superlattices
articles.excerpt_original: Rhombohedral graphene/hBN moiré superlattices exhibit flat-band-driven emergent phases, including superconductivity and the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect (FQAHE), yet the microscopic role of the moiré potential remains unclear. Here, using scanning tunneling microscopy, we visualize moiré-modulated spatial renormalization of flat bands in rhombohedral pentalayer and tetralayer graphene/hBN superlattices. We observe spatially hierarchical filling, manifested as periodic energy shifts of the flat bands at the moiré scale, leading to spatial reshaping of correlated states in the interacting regime. Remarkably, this modulation vanishes below a ~10 nm moiré period--the same threshold below which the FQAHE is absent. Theoretical modeling attributes this mechanism to atomic-corrugation-induced charge redistribution. Our work provides real-space visualization of moiré-engineered flat-band reconstruction, resolving a key link between moiré periodic potential and emergent topological order.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used scanning tunneling microscopy to directly image moiré-scale spatial reshaping of flat bands in rhombohedral graphene/hBN superlattices. They identify a ~10 nm moiré-period threshold linked to the disappearance of the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect, clarifying how atomic corrugation influences correlated topological states.

articles.title_original: Engineering Plasmons in Oxide/Graphene Heterostructures via Interfacial Charge Transfer
articles.title_en: Oxide Overlayers Tune and Stabilize Graphene Plasmons
articles.excerpt_original: Interfacial charge transfer provides an effective route for tailoring the optical and electronic properties of two-dimensional materials. Here, we investigate infrared surface plasmon polaritons in oxide/graphene heterostructures using scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy. Ultrathin oxide overlayers deposited by physical vapor deposition enable systematic engineering of graphene plasmons through interfacial charge redistribution. MoOx strongly enhances the plasmonic response, producing a longer plasmon wavelength, stronger fringe contrast, and reduced damping, whereas a subsequently deposited ZnOx overlayer partially reverses these changes. Energy-dependent nano-infrared imaging combined with quantitative modeling reveals an increased graphene carrier density and the resulting modification of the plasmon dispersion. Thickness-dependent measurements show a rapid increase in charge-transfer doping at sub-nanometer MoOx thicknesses, followed by a weaker long-range contribution at larger overlayer thicknesses. Electrostatic gating further modulates the carrier density and produces a nonlinear response consistent with gate-dependent interfacial charge redistribution. In addition, an approximately 3-nm-thick MoOx overlayer stabilizes the plasmonic response for at least seven months under ambient conditions. These results establish oxide/graphene heterostructures as a robust platform compatible with scalable fabrication, providing a pathway toward stable and tunable infrared nanophotonic and optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered graphene plasmon dispersion and damping by depositing ultrathin MoOx and ZnOx overlayers, using interfacial charge transfer to modulate carrier density. MoOx produced stronger, longer-wavelength plasmon responses and remained stable for at least seven months, supporting tunable infrared nanophotonic and optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: An exploration of the ultrasonication effect on interlayer spacing and mass transfer in Ti3C2 MXene for enhanced CO2 adsorption
articles.title_en: Ultrasonication Enhances CO₂ Adsorption in Ti₃C₂ MXene
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes, particularly Ti 3 C 2 , are promising materials for CO 2 adsorption due to their high surface area, tunable interlayer spacing, and surface functionalization potential. This study investigates the effect of ultrasound-assisted synthesis of Ti 3 C 2 MXene on CO 2 adsorption, which is enhanced through increased interlayer separation and improved mass transfer coefficients. Ultrasonication promotes defect formation and delamination, improving the material’s adsorption efficiency. The adsorption process was analyzed using five isotherm models; among them, the Sips model provided the best fitting R 2 of 0.9925, indicating a combination of monolayer and multilayer adsorption. Adsorption kinetics were evaluated using four models, with the Elovich model showing the highest correlation R 2 of 0.9936, suggesting that physisorption plays a dominant role. Thermodynamic analysis for MXene Ti 3 C 2 treated by ultrasonic confirmed that the CO 2 adsorption process is exothermic and spontaneous with a ΔH of − 8.986 kJ/mol with a negative entropy of − 0.003 kJ/mol·K and ∆G of − 8.241 kJ/mol, indicating structured CO 2 binding and enhanced adsorption stability. Ultrasonication significantly improved adsorption performance by increasing surface area and active site availability, leading to a maximum CO 2 adsorption capacity of 9.990 mmol/g at 25 °C and 9 bar. Additionally, mass transfer analysis revealed rapid initial CO 2 uptake, stabilizing at equilibrium. The enhanced CO 2 uptake and the stability and recyclability of Ti 3 C 2 MXene demonstrate its potential for scalable CO 2 capture applications. Further optimization of synthesis conditions and functionalization strategies could enhance performance, selectivity, and long-term applicability in industrial CO 2 separation and stor
articles.summary_en: Ultrasonication increased Ti₃C₂ MXene interlayer spacing, surface area, and mass transfer, delivering a reported CO₂ adsorption capacity of 9.990 mmol/g at 25 °C and 9 bar. The findings support MXene-based materials for potentially scalable CO₂ capture and separation, although further optimization is needed.

articles.title_original: Direct low-temperature deposition of graphene on an insulator via hydrogen-assisted sputtering
articles.title_en: Hydrogen-Assisted Sputtering Deposits Graphene Directly on Insulators at Low Temperatures
articles.excerpt_original: In this study, the direct growth of graphene on insulating substrates was performed at low temperatures (500-700 {degree sign}C) using hydrogen-assisted sputter deposition (HyAS) with an Ar/H2 gas mixture and a graphite target. Using this approach, few-layer {002}-oriented graphene was formed on SiO2/Si substrates without the use of catalysts or transfer processes. The resulting film exhibited an electrical conductivity of 123 S cm−1 (sheet resistance of 4.07 × 104 Ω/□), hole mobility of 24.5 cm2 V−1 s−1, and carrier concentration of 3.14 × 1019 cm−3. By systematically varying the substrate temperature and hydrogen gas fraction, four distinct regions were identified, corresponding to graphene growth, carbon nanowalls, amorphous carbon, and no film deposition. The study findings suggested that the generation of CHx species by chemical sputtering of the graphite target played an important role in graphene growth, and that the growth mechanism was governed by the balance between the surface decomposition of CHx on the heated substrate and the hydrogen-induced etching of unstable carbon atoms. This approach therefore represents a simple and scalable route for transfer-free graphene integration on insulators at reduced temperatures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated catalyst- and transfer-free deposition of few-layer graphene on SiO₂/Si substrates at 500–700 °C using hydrogen-assisted sputtering. articles.excerpt_original: Abstract This study investigates a novel nanolubricant consisting of Ti3C2Tx MXene as an additive dispersed in polyalkylene glycol (PAG) oil. Nanolubricants containing Ti3C2Tx at mass fractions of 0.1 wt.% and 0.5 wt.% were prepared and evaluated under reciprocating sliding conditions to assess the coefficient of friction and wear performance. Compared to pure PAG (coefficient of friction, COF = 0.197), the 0.1 wt.% formulation yielded a COF of 0.113, while the 0.5 wt.% formulation produced a COF of 0.142. Both nanobricants produced substantial reductions in wear volume in the range of 84 to 89%. Scanning electron microscopy results revealed the formation of tribofilms composed of platelets of Ti3C2Tx on the surface of the metallic counterbody, with evidence of lamellar sheet accommodation within asperity valleys and smoothing of surface roughness. The superior performance of PAG-MXenes nanolubricants is attributed to efficient tribofilm formation, favorable dispersion stability in the polar PAG medium, and optimized interfacial adhesion that minimizes both abrasive and adhesive wear. The results demonstrate that Ti3C2Tx is an effective antiwear additive for PAG-based lubricants, and they highlight the importance of additive mass fraction on tribofilm morphology and tribological outcomes. These findings demonstrate a strong potential of MXenes as effective additives to improve lubrication under harsh operating conditions, offering a transformative approach in tribological applications and encouraging future innovative lubricant approaches. Also, the study highlights the PAG-MXenes combination as an innovative nanolubricant for improving demanding tribology applications.
articles.summary_en: Academic research reports that Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene dispersed in polyalkylene glycol lubricant reduced friction by up to 43% and wear volume by 84–89% in reciprocating sliding tests. articles.title_original: Josephson effect in bipolar magnetic semiconductors
articles.title_en: Bipolar Magnetic Semiconductors Enable Electrically Tunable Josephson Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: We theoretically investigate equilibrium currents in a one-dimensional Josephson junction incorporating a bipolar magnetic semiconductor (BMS). We show that the intrinsic exchange splitting of the spin-resolved bands enables purely electrical control of the $0$--$π$ transition through gate-tunable modulation of the BMS chemical potential, eliminating the need for an external magnetic field. This provides a viable route toward electrically tunable $π$-junction behavior and highlights the potential of BMS-based Josephson devices for phase-controllable superconducting electronics. Furthermore, in the presence of Rashba spin--orbit coupling, we find an anomalous Josephson effect characterized by a finite equilibrium supercurrent at zero phase difference. This behavior originates from the intrinsic breaking of time-reversal symmetry associated with the spin-polarized electronic structure of the BMS. Interestingly, despite the simultaneous breaking of time-reversal and inversion symmetries---conditions often associated with nonreciprocal superconducting transport---we do not observe a Josephson diode effect. Our results therefore highlight an important distinction between anomalous Josephson transport and superconducting nonreciprocity: the former does not necessarily imply a finite critical-current asymmetry between opposite current directions.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical work shows that gate-controlled chemical-potential modulation in bipolar magnetic semiconductors can electrically switch Josephson junctions between 0 and π states without an external magnetic field. Rashba spin–orbit coupling also produces anomalous supercurrents, although not a Josephson diode effect, highlighting potential for phase-controllable superconducting electronics.

articles.title_original: Switchable Triple-Mode Terahertz Polarization Control Based on a Hybrid Graphene-VO2 Metasurface
articles.title_en: Hybrid Graphene–VO2 Metasurface Enables Triple-Mode Terahertz Polarization Control
articles.excerpt_original: We propose a gold-graphene-vanadium dioxide (VO2) hybrid metasurface capable of reversibly switching among three operational modes in the terahertz regime. The device achieves flexible polarization control by combining the insulator-to-metal phase transition of VO2 with the electrical tunability of graphene. Simulation results reveal three distinct behaviors depending on the biasing conditions of the materials. With graphene held at a chemical potential of 0 eV and VO2 in the insulating state, the metasurface acts as a linear-to-linear polarization converter. The polarization conversion ratio (PCR) exceeds 0.9 over the frequency range from 5.5 to 8.6 THz. When the graphene chemical potential is raised to 0.9 eV while VO2 remains insulating, the metasurface switches to linear-to-circular conversion. Notably, the handedness of the outgoing wave depends on the polarization of the incoming signal. Over the 6.45–8.36 THz band, the axial ratio (AR) remains below 3 dB. A third functional state emerges when VO2 switches to its metallic phase. In this state, the device simply operates as a broadband co-polarized reflector, covering the terahertz communication band from 0.1 to 10 THz. This switchable, multifunctional behavior should prove useful for terahertz communications, polarization imaging, and sensing applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a gold–graphene–VO2 metasurface that switches among linear polarization conversion, linear-to-circular conversion, and broadband reflection. Simulations indicate high polarization-conversion performance across targeted terahertz bands, supporting potential applications in communications, imaging, and sensing.

articles.title_original: Homo-metal-element mediated surface modification of sapphire for robust epitaxy of wafer-scale single-crystalline 2D semiconductors
articles.title_en: Surface modification enables wafer-scale single-crystal WS₂ and MoS₂ wafers
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) single-crystal wafers have been envisioned as promising channel materials to drive semiconductor technology down to the atomic limit. Although several efforts have been made, wafer-scale single crystal growth with high robustness and efficiency remains challenging. Here, we design a homo-metal-element (W/Mo and Al) surface modification strategy of commercial C/M sapphire inducing a low-symmetry modification layer. This design enables the robust epitaxial growth of 2-inch scale monolayer WS2 or MoS2 single-crystal wafers via a facile chemical vapor deposition (CVD) method. Since no exogenous elements are introduced on the substrate surface, the derived monolayer WS2 single crystals present high crystal quality and no impurity introduction, as evidenced by multi-scale characterizations and field effect transistors array fabrications (on/off ratio >108 and mobility ~48.2 cm2 V−1 s−1). This work should hereby propel the wafer-scale synthesis and the internal epitaxial mechanism exploration of 2D TMDCs single crystals via substrate surface modulation, and promote the high-performance applications in various fields. The wafer-scale growth of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides is desired for their electronic applications. Here, the authors report a surface modification strategy of commercial sapphire substrates to grow wafer-scale monolayer WS2 or MoS2 single crystals, showing their application for high-performance transistors arrays.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a homo-metal-element surface modification of commercial sapphire that enables epitaxial growth of 2-inch monolayer WS₂ and MoS₂ single-crystal wafers by CVD. articles.title_original: MXenes for multifunctional optoelectronics: Advances, challenges, and roadmap
articles.title_en: MXene Review Maps a Roadmap for Multifunctional Optoelectronics
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes have emerged as transformative materials for optoelectronic applications, yet interfacial complexities and stability challenges restrict their full potential. While numerous studies have explored MXenes in individual devices, a unified perspective linking their material chemistry to multifunctional optoelectronic systems remains limited. This review provides a critical framework that connects MXene composition, surface terminations, and defect chemistry to device-level performance across four complementary pillars of optoelectronics: photovoltaics, photodetectors, neuromorphic devices, and light-emitting diodes. Together, these platforms represent the full functional cycle of light harvesting, sensing, information processing, and emission. We analyze how material synthesis routes and surface engineering govern interfacial energetics, charge transport, and switching dynamics, enabling MXenes to act as electrodes, charge-transport layers, and active components. By establishing the structure–property–device framework, we identify key chemical and environmental bottlenecks that hinder industrial scalability and propose a strategic roadmap toward durable, high-throughput MXene-based optoelectronic systems.
articles.summary_en: A review links MXene composition, surface terminations, and defect chemistry to performance in photovoltaics, photodetectors, neuromorphic devices, and light-emitting diodes. articles.title_original: Nonlocal-nonlinear phonon polaritons
articles.title_en: Study identifies nonlocal nonlinear phonon-polariton interactions in polar crystals
articles.excerpt_original: When light is confined to deeply subwavelength volumes, optical responses can become nonlocal. Yet how nonlocality reshapes nonlinear light-matter interactions remains largely unexplored, particularly in dielectrics. Here, we theoretically uncover a new class of nonlinear optical processes arising from the interplay between optical-phonon propagation and ionic-bond anharmonicity in polar crystals. We show that, unlike conventional local nonlinearities, this mechanism enables second-order responses even in centrosymmetric materials. Moreover, these responses can be tuned by the confinement and resonantly enhanced near optical-phonon resonances. Using density functional perturbation theory, we quantify the resulting nonlocal second-order susceptibilities in representative polar crystals. Our results establish nonlocal-nonlinear optics as a new regime of light-matter interaction in dielectrics.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical research shows that optical-phonon propagation and ionic-bond anharmonicity can produce tunable second-order optical responses in centrosymmetric polar crystals. articles.title_original: Acousto-electric current in graphene under the influence of electromagnetic waves
articles.title_en: Quantum Model Explores Acousto-Electric Current Control in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional graphene has garnered significant interest owing to its unique quantum behaviors stemming from a linear energy dispersion relation, with the acoustic-electric (AE) effect emerging as a key phenomenon driven by charge carrier dynamics under surface acoustic waves (SAW). Classical models based on the Boltzmann kinetic equation, effective at elevated temperatures, fall short in accounting for low-temperature experimental data. This work adopts the quantum kinetic equation approach to analyze the AE current in monolayer graphene subjected to combined SAW and electromagnetic waves (EMW). We derive an analytical formula for the AE current that fully captures the electron-acoustic phonon scattering via the deformation potential mechanism and elucidates SAW's role. Numerical simulations reveal the AE current's nonlinear rise with temperature, alongside sharp declines with increasing material sound velocity and EMW parameters. These trends highlight the potential for precise control of AE current via external stimuli. By advancing from classical to quantum frameworks, this study offers deeper insights into the AE effect's fundamentals in two-dimensional graphene.

articles.title_original: Systems Progress Overview of ROSISat: The Radiation Orbital Shielding Investigation Satellite
articles.title_en: ROSISat to Test Radiation-Shielding Materials in Orbit
articles.excerpt_original: Exposure to space weather in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) space weather environment poses significant challenges to both the integrity and longevity of orbital hardware, as well as the health of astronauts, driving the necessity for improved means of radiation shielding for future manned and unmanned missions. With a 1U CubeSat formfactor, ROSISat is a planned LEO mission that aims to characterize the radiation shielding capabilities of seven candidate materials. By comparing the shielding performance of each composite and constituent material, ROSISat will place a specific focus on correlating how molecular structure influences radiation shielding. Further, current simulations lack the fidelity to account for differences in molecular structure when analyzing shielding properties, thus emphasizing the necessity of in-situ testing. With one paired with each cell, nine SRAM computer memory modules will be embedded beneath the 3x3 aluminum material attachment plate, while onboard microcontrollers will monitor and quantify the bitflips occurring with each material. This will allow the radiation dose rate received by each module to be assessed for material comparison, providing greater understanding of how molecular structure influences the shielding capabilities of composite materials. The general space environment for various LEO orbits is being modeled using the Ansys STK software. Testing initiatives, including a future high-altitude balloon flight, will be conducted to verify subsystem designs and functionality. The ROSISat mission is projected to be flight-ready by 2028, with direct implications for future Earth-orbiting missions, including advancing the strength and reliability of shielding for EVA suits, manned craft, and long-term habitats.
articles.summary_en: The planned 1U ROSISat CubeSat will compare seven candidate materials and composites by measuring radiation-induced SRAM bit flips in low Earth orbit. articles.title_original: Hartree--Fock coercivity for twisted bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Study Establishes Hartree–Fock Coercivity in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We study the minimisers of the Hartree--Fock functional for flat bands in the chiral model of twisted bilayer graphene introduced by Tarnopolsky, Kruchkov, and Vishwanath. Our model is a continuous version of the discrete model considered by Becker, Lin and Stubbs in previous works and the first result is a direct analogue of main theorems of those papers: at half filling of the flat band of multiplicity two, there are exactly two minimisers, obtained by occupying either one of the two sub-bands. (A more general version of this result, stressing its topological origins, was presented in Appendix A.8 of the Lecture Notes by Tao-Zworski.) The new contribution is the strict coercivity of the Hessian of the Hartree--Fock functional at the two minimisers. It is a consequence of the difference between the Chern numbers of the component bands and can be optimistically considered as a soft version of a ``spectral gap''.
articles.summary_en: Academic research analyzes Hartree–Fock minimizers in the flat bands of chiral twisted bilayer graphene. articles.title_original: Exploring two-phonon Raman scattering in bilayer graphene by carbon isotope labelling
articles.title_en: Isotope labelling reveals interlayer coupling in bilayer graphene Raman scattering
articles.excerpt_original: The scattering processes of Raman modes in monolayer graphene have been extensively discussed, whereas they become more complex in bilayer graphene due to interlayer interaction. Here, we present a Raman study of bilayer graphene utilizing isotope labeling to investigate significant two-phonon scattering processes. Our findings reveal that the G*, 2D, and 2D′ modes can be explicitly decoupled into three components originating from the top layer, the bottom layer, and both layers combined. This indicates that the scattering processes of all three modes inherently involve interlayer electron–phonon coupling. Furthermore, as the twist angle of bilayer graphene increases, the proportion of these interlayer scattering components exhibits a non-monotonic evolution. The local enhancement of the interlayer components closely tracks the line shape broadening of the two-phonon mode, which is fundamentally driven by the resonance between the emitted photon energy and the energy gap of the Van Hove singularities. Importantly, we clarify that this optically derived interlayer electron–phonon coupling fraction should be distinguished from the static structural van der Waals interaction strength. This work establishes a more comprehensive framework for analyzing the Raman spectra of graphene under diverse conditions, advancing the utility of Raman spectroscopy in probing the intricate physical properties of low-dimensional 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers use carbon isotope labelling to separate two-phonon Raman contributions from each graphene layer and their combined response. The study links twist-angle-dependent changes and spectral broadening to interlayer electron–phonon coupling, improving Raman analysis of bilayer graphene.

The study was conducted using a composite comprising chitosan (Cs), fish collagen (FC), MXene, Zirconium oxide (ZrO₂), and Copper (Cu). In this study, the nanocomposite was incorporated into wound dressing patches using an environmentally friendly gel-casting method. In particular, the combination of MXene nanosheets with bioactive metal-ion-incorporated patches exhibited enhanced mechanical strength, stability, and moisture retention. Moreover, the Cs/FC/MXene/ZrO₂+Cu showed excellent cytocompatibility, hemocompatibility, and antibacterial activity in in vitro conditions. The in vivo studies were performed using streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice with full-thickness wounds. Furthermore, the histopathological examination showed that the treated wounds developed thick collagen networks, exhibited granulation tissue, increased angiogenesis, and decreased inflammation compared with the control groups. Collectively, the combination of MXene with bioactive metal composite produced enhanced wound-healing outcomes through synergistic effects. The developed nanocomposite-incorporated patch demonstrates significant therapeutic potential to mitigate the clinical and socioeconomic burdens associated with chronic and diabetic ulcers. Chronic and diabetic wounds require innovative tissue repair therapies. Here,an MXene-based nanocomposite patch enhanced biocompatibility, antibacterial activity, and diabetic wound healing in vitro and in vivo.

articles.title_original: Halogen Surface Terminations in Ti 3 C 2 MXenes for Interface Engineering in Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.title_en: Halogen-Terminated MXenes Improve Perovskite Solar-Cell Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Halogen surface functionalization has emerged as a promising strategy to modulate MXene properties. However, most reported MXenes exhibit heterogeneous surface terminations (), hindering the establishment of clear correlations between structure and electronic properties. Here, delaminated MXenes with controlled –Cl and –Br terminations are investigated to elucidate the relationship between surface chemistry and the electronic and optical response. To explore their impact on optoelectronic devices, the MXenes are employed as dopants in an IT‐4F interfacial layer positioned between the electron transport layer and the perovskite absorber in n‐i‐p architectures. A combined theoretical and experimental approach is used to investigate the role of halogen terminations in modulating MXene and interfacial layer properties. While limited effects are observed in planar devices, mesoscopic solar cells based on FTO/c‐/m‐//PEAI/PTAA/Au exhibit improved performance upon incorporation of 1 vol% MXene in IT‐4F, with Br‐terminated yielding the highest average power conversion efficiency (15.44 0.21%) and a champion efficiency of 17.06%. These findings highlight the influence of halogen surface terminations on MXene properties and device performance.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated controlled chlorine and bromine surface terminations in Ti₃C₂ MXenes used as dopants in an interfacial layer for perovskite solar cells. Bromine-terminated MXenes produced the strongest results in mesoscopic devices, reaching a champion power-conversion efficiency of 17.06%.

articles.title_original: Synergistic enhancement of bioepoxy composites via MXene-functionalised coir fibres: mechanical and thermal properties evaluation
articles.title_en: MXene-Functionalised Coir Fibres Enhance Bioepoxy Composites
articles.summary_en: Researchers evaluated MXene-functionalised coir fibres in bioepoxy composites, reporting synergistic improvements in mechanical and thermal properties. The work highlights a potential route to higher-performance, bio-based composite materials.

articles.title_original: Review: MXenes for energy storage and conversion devices—advances in green synthesis, use of machine-learning, and electrochemical response
articles.title_en: Review surveys MXenes for energy storage and conversion
articles.summary_en: This review examines advances in green MXene synthesis, machine-learning applications, and electrochemical performance for energy storage and conversion devices. It highlights research directions for improving material production and device response, without identifying a specific commercial deployment.

articles.title_original: Interface-Engineered MXene/TMD Heterostructures for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution: Progress, DFT-Guided Mechanisms, and Perspectives
articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene/TMD Heterostructures for Hydrogen Evolution
articles.excerpt_original: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) requires efficient, durable, and earth-abundant electrocatalysts to reduce reliance on platinum-group metals. MXene/transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures offer a promising platform by combining the abundant, tunable catalytic sites of TMDs with the high electrical conductivity, hydrophilicity, and versatile surface chemistry of MXenes. This review critically examines recent advances in the synthesis, interfacial engineering, and HER performance of MXene/TMD heterostructures, with particular emphasis on how interfacial interactions govern catalytic behavior. The roles of phase engineering, defect and heteroatom incorporation, surface terminations, and heterointerface construction are discussed in relation to interfacial charge redistribution, electronic-structure modulation, hydrogen adsorption energetics, active-site accessibility, and reaction kinetics. Experimental HER performance across representative MXene/TMD systems is compared to establish structure-interface-performance relationships and identify the origins of enhanced activity and stability. Particular attention is given to density functional theory (DFT) as a mechanistic tool for resolving heterostructure stability, interfacial charge transfer, electronic structure, and hydrogen adsorption free energy (ΔGH*). The review also assesses limitations in current computational descriptions of electrocatalytic interfaces, including solvent and electrolyte effects, potential-dependent surface charging, dynamic surface reconstruction, and the accuracy of commonly used exchange-correlation functionals. By integrating experimental observations with theoretical insights, this review identifies interfacial electronic coupling and local active-site chemistry as central
articles.summary_en: This academic review assesses MXene/transition-metal dichalcogenide heterostructures as platinum-sparing electrocatalysts for hydrogen evolution. It emphasizes interface engineering, charge transfer, active-site chemistry, and DFT-guided mechanisms, while noting limitations in current computational models.

articles.title_original: High mobility p -type doping of hexagonal boron nitride films on diamond (100) substrates
articles.title_en: Magnesium-Doped h-BN Enables High-Mobility p-Type Films on Diamond
articles.excerpt_original: The heteroepitaxy of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) on diamond exhibits significant potential for the advancement of diamond-based electronic devices. p-Type doping of h-BN is expected to provide sufficient carriers for forming a two-dimensional hole gas at the diamond interfaces. However, high-mobility doping of h-BN remains challenging. Here, we report the in situ growth of magnesium-doped h-BN films on single-crystal diamond (100) substrates using radio frequency magnetron sputtering, followed by an annealing treatment in the same vacuum chamber. The resultant h-BN films exhibit dense and atomically smooth surfaces with roughness below 1 nm, as well as uniform doping profiles within the films. Both x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and secondary ion mass spectroscopy reveal the presence of Mg–N bonds, suggesting the successful incorporation of Mg atoms. The successive annealing treatment after growth further improved the activation efficiency of the dopants. Hall effect measurements revealed distinct p-type conductivity, with hole mobility increasing to 222 cm2/V s and resistivity decreasing by over three orders of magnitude. These results demonstrate an effective and feasible route for achieving high-mobility p-type h-BN films directly on diamond substrates, which are essential for developing high-performance diamond-based electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated in situ magnesium doping of hexagonal boron nitride films on diamond substrates, achieving hole mobility of 222 cm²/V·s and a more than three-order reduction in resistivity. The advance supports development of two-dimensional hole gases and high-performance diamond-based electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Probing microstructural modification and hardness response in h-BN reinforced A356 aluminum matrix composites
articles.title_en: h-BN Reinforcement Improves Hardness of A356 Aluminum Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract A356 Al-Si-Mg alloys are widely used in lightweight structural applications; however, their as-cast mechanical performance is strongly influenced by the morphology of dendritic α-Al, the interconnected eutectic Si-rich network, and casting-induced microstructural heterogeneity. In this study, A356 aluminum matrix composites containing 1 and 4 wt.% hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) were fabricated by induction melting to investigate the effect of h-BN addition on microstructural evolution and localized hardness. The composites were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), FESEM, Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping, semiquantitative image analysis, and Vickers microhardness testing. XRD analysis showed that α-Al and Si remained the dominant crystalline phases, with no distinct reaction products detected. SEM observations and image analysis indicated that h-BN addition reduced the apparent continuity of the interdendritic eutectic Si-rich network, with the median major-axis length of the segmented Si-rich features decreasing from 3.38 µm in the unreinforced A356 alloy to 3.14 µm and 2.72 µm in the composites containing 1 and 4 wt.% h-BN, respectively. EDS mapping qualitatively confirmed the presence of B-containing regions in the reinforced composites. The mean Vickers hardness increased from 57.5 HV to 64.4 HV and 71 HV with increasing h-BN content, corresponding to improvements of approximately 12% and 23.5%, respectively. The hardness enhancement is primarily attributed to eutectic Si network modification, with possible additional contributions from localized restriction of plastic deformation. Overall, the results establish a processing-microstructure-hardness relationship in cast A356/h-BN composites and demonstrate that h-BN addition improves local
articles.summary_en: Academic research shows that adding 1–4 wt.% hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) to cast A356 aluminum modifies the eutectic silicon network and increases Vickers hardness by approximately 12% and 23.5%, respectively. The findings establish a processing–microstructure–hardness relationship for lightweight structural composites, though no company or commercial application is identified.

articles.title_original: Semiconductor-to-metal transition and interconnect parameter optimization in noble metal passivated AlNNR: A density functional theory approach
articles.title_en: DFT study optimizes noble-metal-passivated aluminum nitride nanoribbon interconnects
articles.excerpt_original: Aluminum nitride nanoribbons (AlNNR) passivated with silver (Ag) and gold (Au) atoms at single-atom and double-atom edge configurations have been systematically investigated. Structural, electronic, and interconnect properties are evaluated using first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The structural analysis reveals that 2-atom passivated configurations exhibit greater thermodynamic stability. It is evidenced by more negative total energies. Single-atom up-passivated systems demonstrate superior binding energies. Au-up passivation structure yields the most stable of −6.66 eV. Electronic characterization through band structure and projected density of states (PDOS) analysis confirms that single-atom passivated AlNNR configurations exhibit semiconducting behavior with band gaps ranging from 0.65 eV to 1.00 eV. Bilateral 2-atom passivation induces a semiconductor-to-metal transition. Interconnect parameter analysis demonstrates that up-passivated configurations possess significantly reduced RC delays of approximately 43–64 μs and enhanced Fermi velocities. It makes them highly suitable candidates for nanoscale interconnect applications. The charge redistribution governs through metal passivant d -orbitals and nitrogen p-orbitals. Edge-selective metal passivation shows a viable structures for engineering nanoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: A density functional theory study examines aluminum nitride nanoribbons passivated with silver or gold atoms, finding that bilateral two-atom passivation can induce a semiconductor-to-metal transition. The modeled structures show improved interconnect parameters, including reduced RC delays and higher Fermi velocities, suggesting potential for nanoscale electronics.

articles.title_original: Nanofabrication techniques and lithography process
articles.title_en: Review of Nanofabrication Techniques and Lithography Processes
articles.excerpt_original: Nanofabrication is the foundation of modern nanotechnology, enabling the creation of devices with sub-100 nm features for applications in electronics, medicine, energy, and sensing. This chapter reviews both top-down and bottom-up approaches, outlining their principles, advantages, and limitations. Top-down methods, such as photolithography, electron beam lithography (EBL), nano-thermal patterning, and focused ion beam (FIB) milling, shape bulk materials into nanoscale structures. Bottom-up techniques, such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD), atomic layer deposition, solution-based deposition, electrochemical methods, and self-assembly, build materials atom-by-atom or molecule-by-molecule. Thin-film deposition methods—physical vapor deposition (PVD), CVD, and related variants—are discussed with emphasis on their process physics, material compatibility, and application scope. This chapter also highlights material classes for nanodevices, ranging from semiconductors and magnetic thin films to carbon-based nanomaterials, 2D materials, and quantum materials. Key challenges in scalability, defect control, material integration, device reliability, and cost are addressed, along with mitigation strategies. Applications in nanoelectronics, nanomedicine, energy harvesting, storage, sensors, and actuators illustrate the transformative potential of nanofabrication. By integrating advanced materials, precise fabrication techniques, and innovative design strategies, nanofabrication continues to push the limits of device miniaturization, enabling next-generation technologies and groundbreaking advancements across industry, science, and society.
articles.summary_en: This academic chapter reviews top-down and bottom-up nanofabrication methods for producing sub-100 nm structures, including lithography, deposition, electrochemical processing, and self-assembly. It assesses material compatibility, scalability, defect control, integration, reliability, and applications in nanoelectronics, medicine, energy storage, sensing, and actuators.

articles.title_original: Electrical transport and low-frequency noise in MoS2 field-effect transistors under controlled gas atmospheres
articles.title_en: MoS2 Transistors Reveal Gas-Adsorption Noise Mechanisms
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional semiconductors, and particularly MoS2, are promising active materials for room-temperature gas sensing devices because their channel conductance is strongly modulated by surface adsorption. Here we report a systematic study of the electrical transport properties of back-gated MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) under controlled atmosphere and pressure. Transferred MoS2 devices show stable n-type operation with a pronounced dependence of conductance, threshold voltage and hysteresis on ambient conditions, consistent with adsorption/desorption and trap dynamics at the MoS2/SiO2 interface. To further clarify the microscopic kinetics underlying these macroscopic electrical variations, we performed low-frequency noise measurements. The spectra exhibit a 1/f^γ background and Lorentzian components whose characteristic frequencies are in the tens-of-hertz range (≈ 40 – 60 Hz) and at ~2.0 kHz. The slow component shows thermally activated behaviour with E_a≈0.19 eV, consistent with physisorption-controlled dynamics, while the faster component is compatible with contact-related fluctuations. Measurements on CVD-grown MoS2 FETs reproduce the same slow fluctuations, supporting the generality of the adsorption-driven process. Overall, this work establishes a solid transport baseline for MoS2 FETs in controlled atmospheres and demonstrates that low-frequency noise spectroscopy provides a powerful tool to disentangle surface-adsorption kinetics from contact and interface effects.
articles.summary_en: Researchers characterized transport and low-frequency noise in back-gated MoS2 field-effect transistors under controlled atmospheres. The findings clarify adsorption, interface-trap, and contact-related fluctuations relevant to room-temperature gas sensing and semiconductor device development.

articles.title_original: MXene Chemistries for Biomedicine: On-Body, In-Body, and Beyond
articles.title_en: Review Maps MXene Chemistries Across Biomedical Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXenes, a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition-metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, have gained considerable attention as highly versatile nanomaterials for biomedical applications owing to their high electrical conductivity, chemically tunable surfaces, mixed ionic–electronic transport, and controllable redox activity. This review provides a structured overview of MXene-based biomedical technologies, organized by their functional interaction with the human body. We first examine on-body applications, highlighting MXene-enabled wearable, epidermal, and implantable bioelectronics. We then discuss in-body applications, including regenerative medicine, advanced cancer therapies, and antimicrobial strategies, emphasizing how MXene chemistry regulates biological interactions and therapeutic performance. Finally, we address applications outside the body, such as biosensing and diagnostic platforms, where MXenes enhance sensitivity, signal transduction, and imaging capabilities. Beyond summarizing recent advances, this review critically analyzes current gaps in knowledge, including long-term biocompatibility, degradation pathways, immune interactions, and structure–activity relationships, which currently limit clinical translation. We conclude by outlining key future directions, including sustainable synthesis, oxidation-resistant and fluorine-free MXenes, and the integration of artificial intelligence to accelerate materials discovery and application-specific design. Together, these insights position MXenes as chemistry-programmable nanoplatforms with strong potential to bridge on-body, in-body, and outside-the-body biomedical technologies.
articles.summary_en: An ACS review examines MXenes in wearable and implantable bioelectronics, regenerative medicine, cancer therapy, antimicrobial strategies, biosensing, and diagnostics. It identifies biocompatibility, degradation, immune interactions, and synthesis sustainability as key barriers to clinical translation.

articles.title_original: Deep-Eutectic-Solvent-Enabled Polyampholyte/MXene Eutectogels for Environmentally Tolerant Wearable Respiratory Monitoring
articles.title_en: DES-Enabled MXene Eutectogel Advances Wearable Respiratory Monitoring
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Conductive hydrogels are promising for wearable electronics; however, freezing and dehydration of their water-rich networks often compromise mechanical compliance, electrical conductivity, and sensing reliability. Here, we report a deep-eutectic-solvent-enabled polyampholyte/MXene eutectogel constructed from a betaine/ethylene glycol deep eutectic solvent (DES), a dynamically crosslinked polyampholyte network formed from sodium p-styrenesulfonate (NaSS) and quaternized dimethylaminoethyl acrylate (DMAEA-Q), and MXene nanosheets. MXene establishes the principal conductive pathways, while DES-mediated molecular interactions alter the local electronic structure of representative polyampholyte-associated complexes. Density functional theory calculations show that replacing water with DES redistributes the frontier molecular orbitals and decreases the calculated HOMO–LUMO energy difference of the NaSS-DMAEA-Q complex from 4.60 to 4.34 eV, consistent with a more favorable local charge-transfer environment. Correspondingly, at the same MXene loading, the DES-based eutectogel reaches a conductivity of 1.51 S/m, more than twice that of the water-based hydrogel (0.71 S/m). The DES hydrogen-bonding network also suppresses crystallization and solvent evaporation, while reversible ionic-pair interactions provide high deformability and adhesion. This formulation exhibits a fracture strain of approximately 630%, an adhesion strength of 47.9 kPa, a crystallization peak at –74.3 °C, and 94% mass retention after 30 days. The resulting sensor enables strain, pressure, temperature, and respiratory monitoring. Furthermore, integration with an STM32-based signal-acquisition system and a deep neural network enables four-class recognition of respiratory signals collected from the mout
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers developed a deep-eutectic-solvent polyampholyte/MXene eutectogel that maintains conductivity, adhesion, deformability, and mass retention across challenging temperature and hydration conditions. The material enabled multimodal sensing of strain, pressure, temperature, and respiration, with neural-network signal recognition.

articles.title_original: Controlled Synthesis of Tri‐ and Multi‐Doped Graphene
articles.title_en: Review Surveys Controlled Synthesis of Tri- and Multi-Doped Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Graphene possesses exceptional electrical, mechanical, and thermal properties, yet its lack of a bandgap and chemically inert surface continue to limit practical applications. Heteroatom doping has emerged as the primary strategy to overcome these limitations by tuning graphene's electronic structure and creating catalytically active sites. While single‐ and dual‐doped graphene systems are now well established, tri‐ and multi‐doped graphene remain comparatively underexplored, despite their potential to generate cooperative electronic interactions and highly tunable active‐site configurations. This review critically examines recent advances in the controlled synthesis of tri‐ and multi‐doped graphene systems. We compare bottom‐up approaches, including pyrolysis, hydrothermal synthesis, and flash Joule heating, with top‐down post‐synthetic modification methods, focusing on how synthesis conditions govern dopant incorporation, bonding configuration, defect formation, and structural ordering. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationship between dopant configuration and resulting catalytic, electrocatalytic, energy‐storage, and sensing performance. The review highlights that dopant proximity and local bonding environment are often more important than dopant number alone. Finally, current limitations in scalability, atomic‐level control, and reproducibility are discussed together with emerging strategies for rational multi‐dopant engineering.
articles.summary_en: The review examines bottom-up and post-synthetic methods for incorporating multiple heteroatoms into graphene, focusing on dopant configuration, bonding, defects and structural order. It links these factors to catalytic, energy-storage and sensing performance while highlighting persistent challenges in scalability, atomic-level control and reproducibility.

articles.title_original: Asymmetric strain distribution in ferroelectric/paraelectric SnTe-PbTe monolayer lateral heterostructures
articles.title_en: STM Maps Asymmetric Strain in SnTe–PbTe Monolayer Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Monolayer lateral heterostructures (LHSs) composed of two-dimensional semiconducting ferroelectrics hold promise for non-volatile electronic and optoelectronic applications. Lattice misfit strain at these atomically sharp interfaces can significantly modulate in-plane polarization and related electronic properties, yet the direct characterization of the strain profile remains challenging. Here, we map the strain in SnTe-PbTe monolayer LHSs quantitatively via low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). By combining moiré pattern simulation and geometric phase analysis, we achieve lattice parameter measurements with 0.02 Å precision—which substantially exceeds conventional STM resolution. Significant tensile strain is observed in SnTe regions, while PbTe sections exhibit much smaller strain. Density functional theory calculations attribute this asymmetric strain distribution to distinct atomic coordination in each monolayer semiconductor. These findings offer critical insights into strain engineering of ultrathin group-IV monochalcogenide heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers quantitatively mapped strain in ferroelectric/paraelectric SnTe–PbTe lateral heterostructures using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy, moiré simulations, and geometric phase analysis. The findings reveal substantially higher tensile strain in SnTe than PbTe, informing strain engineering for ultrathin electronic and optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Gate-tunable negative differential resistance in multifunctional van der Waals heterostructure
articles.title_en: Gate-Tunable Negative Differential Resistance Demonstrated in 2D Semiconductor Heterojunction
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors have emerged as exciting candidates for the development of low-power and multifunctional computing applications, thanks to their qualities such as layer-dependent band gap tunability, high carrier mobility, and excellent electrostatic control. Here, we explore a pair of 2D semiconductors with nearly broken-gap (Type-III-like) band alignment and demonstrate a highly gate-tunable p-MoTe 2 /n-SnS 2 heterojunction with multifunctional behavior. Employing a dual-gated asymmetric device geometry, we unveil its functionality as both a forward and backward rectifying device. Moreover, we observe a highly gate-tunable negative differential resistance (NDR), with a gate-coupling efficiency of η ≃ 0.5 and a peak-to-valley ratio of ∼ 3 down to 150 K. By employing density functional theory, we determine that the observed NDR is dominated by valence band-to-valence band tunneling, while additional interband tunneling contributions arise at higher bias. The combination of tunneling driven transport and gate controllability of NDR opens the pathway for realizing gate-tunable 2D material-based neuromorphic and energy-efficient electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated gate-tunable negative differential resistance and switchable rectification in a p-MoTe₂/n-SnS₂ van der Waals heterojunction. The findings support potential neuromorphic and energy-efficient electronics based on two-dimensional semiconductors.

articles.title_original: Ionizing Radiation Induced Strain Engineering for Exciton Dynamics in Atomically Thin Semiconductor
articles.title_en: Ionizing Radiation Enables Strain Engineering in Monolayer WSe2
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Uncovering and controlling exciton dynamics in atomically thin semiconductors is crucial for excitonic devices. While conventional techiniques often damage materials, ionizing radiation offers a non‐contact, low‐cost modulation method. Here, we introduce a non‐destructive strain‐engineering approach using low‐energy (≤1000 eV) alpha‐particle irradiation in monolayer WSe 2 . The irradiation induces helium accumulation beneath the monolayer, forming defect‐free nanobubbles that can be merged via annealing. These bubbles create an exciton funneling effect, boosting photoluminescence and causing a spectral redshift. The induced strain gradient enhances exciton localization and raises the optimal temperature for emission and transport. This work demonstrates controlled ionizing radiation as a powerful tool for tuning 2D exciton dynamics, with potential for sensing, energy harvesting, and quantum technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used low-energy alpha-particle irradiation to create defect-free nanobubbles beneath monolayer WSe2, producing strain gradients that funnel and localize excitons. The approach enhances photoluminescence and may support future sensing, energy-harvesting, and quantum technologies.

articles.title_original: Microwave Spectroscopy of Few-Carrier States in Bilayer Graphene Quantum Dots
articles.title_en: cQED Spectroscopy Probes Few-Carrier States in Bilayer Graphene Quantum Dots
articles.excerpt_original: Bilayer graphene is a maturing material platform for gate-defined quantum dots that hosts long-lived spin and valley states. Implementing solid-state qubits in bilayer graphene requires a fundamental understanding of such confined electronic systems. In particular, states of two and three carriers, for which the exchange interaction between particles plays a crucial role, are a cornerstone for qubit readout and manipulation. Here we report on the spectroscopy of few-carrier states in bilayer graphene quantum dots, using circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques that offer substantially improved energy resolution compared to standard transport techniques. Measurements of a superconducting high-impedance resonator capacitively coupled to the double quantum dot reveal dispersive features of two- and three-electron states, enabling the detection of Pauli spin and valley blockade and the characterization of the spin-orbit gap at zero magnetic field. The results deepen our understanding of few-carrier spin and valley states in bilayer graphene quantum dots and demonstrate that cQED techniques are a powerful state-selective probe for semiconductor nanostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used circuit quantum electrodynamics to resolve two- and three-electron states in bilayer graphene quantum dots. The measurements detected Pauli spin and valley blockade and characterized the zero-field spin–orbit gap, advancing state-selective readout for graphene-based semiconductor qubits.

articles.title_original: “Interfacial organization of graphene oxide–polyelectrolyte multilayers with tunable memristive behavior”
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Multilayers Demonstrate Tunable Memristive Switching
articles.excerpt_original: Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembled graphene oxide–polyelectrolyte (GO–PE) multilayers were fabricated on indium tin oxide substrates and systematically investigated in terms of structure, morphology, and resistive switching behavior. Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (QCM-D) confirmed controlled and reproducible growth of GO–PDADMAC and GO–PEI structures, with higher mass incorporation observed for the GO–PEI system. UV–Vis spectroscopy revealed the linear increase in absorbance versus bilayer number, confirming uniform film formation and progressive electronic coupling between adjacent GO sheets. Microscopic analysis (SEM and AFM) demonstrated complete substrate coverage after four bilayers and parallel stacking of GO nanoflakes with single-layer thickness of ∼1.1 nm. Increased surface roughness and mass loading in GO–PEI films indicated stronger GO–polyelectrolyte interactions. Electrical characterization showed reproducible bipolar resistive switching with well-defined low- and high-resistance states. A transition from ohmic to space-charge-limited current (SCLC) conduction was observed beyond the switching threshold (±1.2–1.5 V), indicating trap-controlled transport. Pulse measurements demonstrated stable and fully reversible switching up to ±2.4 V. Notably, GO–PEI systems exhibited more gradual and controllable potentiation behavior compared to GO–PDADMAC, highlighting their potential for analog switching and neuromorphic applications. The results establish structure–property relationships in GO-based LbL multilayers and demonstrate their suitability as tunable carbon-based memristive platforms.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated layer-by-layer graphene oxide–polyelectrolyte multilayers with reproducible bipolar resistive switching and reversible operation up to ±2.4 V. Graphene oxide–polyethylenimine films showed more gradual potentiation, supporting potential analog-memory and neuromorphic applications.

articles.title_original: Quantum Hydrodynamic Framework of Coherent Terahertz Emission in MXenes Driven via Engineered Femtosecond Waveforms
articles.title_en: Quantum Framework Targets Coherent THz Emission from MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: Coherent terahertz (THz) emitters based on low dimensional quantum materials have attracted significant interest for compact broadband photonic technologies. However, theoretical descriptions that consistently connect microscopic quantum dynamics to emitted THz radiation remain limited for MXenes, whose electronic properties are governed by transition metal d orbitals and chemically tunable surface terminations. A multiscale density-matrix formalism for coherent THz generation in metallic MXenes driven by engineered three color femtosecond waveforms is developed. Material-specific electronic structures are described by parameterized multiband tight binding Hamiltonians, while ultrafast carrier dynamics are treated using a non-secular Redfield master equation that explicitly retains interband coherence, carrier populations, electron phonon interactions, impurity scattering, and environment-induced relaxation. The transient photocurrent is explicitly decomposed into population and coherence driven contributions and linked to the emitted THz field through its time derivative, establishing a direct connection between microscopic quantum dynamics and macroscopic radiation. The results show that environmental coupling does not merely attenuate THz emission, but redistributes coherent and population currents and reshapes the emitted waveform in both the time and frequency domains. Systematic investigations of optical waveform parameters, effective electronic structure, and open system relaxation identify physically grounded strategies for enhancing broadband THz generation. The proposed methodology establishes a transferable microscopic design platform for connecting material specific electronic structure, quantum coherence, open system relaxation, nonlinear carrier transport,
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a multiscale quantum-hydrodynamic model linking MXene electronic dynamics, environmental interactions, and emitted terahertz radiation. The framework identifies waveform and relaxation strategies for enhancing broadband THz generation in compact photonic technologies.

articles.title_original: Synergistic CdS-MXene-TiO2 ternary nanocomposite with enhanced photomagnetocatalytic degradation under visible-light and its electrochemical properties
articles.title_en: CdS–MXene–TiO₂ Nanocomposite Enhances Visible-Light Photocatalytic Degradation
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a ternary CdS–MXene–TiO₂ nanocomposite with enhanced photomagnetocatalytic degradation under visible light and related electrochemical properties. The work indicates potential for environmental remediation, although the available excerpt provides no performance metrics or application validation.

articles.title_original: Upshifted d-Band Center and Electron Delocalization in High-Entropy MXene Enabling Highly Reversible Anode-Free Sodium Batteries
articles.title_en: High-Entropy MXene Enables Reversible Anode-Free Sodium Batteries
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Anode-free sodium metal batteries (AFSMBs) have attracted significant attention owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density and low-cost advantages. However, their practical application is severely hindered by uncontrolled sodium dendrite growth and unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces. Herein, we propose an interface modification strategy based on high-entropy MXene, (Ti1/5V1/5Zr1/5Nb1/5Ta1/5)2CTx (HE-MXene), to regulate the electronic structure of the current collector. It has been demonstrated that the synergistic interactions among multiple transition metal elements in HE-MXene upshift the d-band center and induce electron delocalization, which effectively enhance sodium ion adsorption and promote uniform charge transfer, ultimately facilitating homogeneous sodium deposition and the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI. As a result, the HE-MXene-modified electrode reduces the sodium nucleation overpotential to 6.2 mV. Specifically, the half-cell achieves stable cycling for over 400 h at 0.5 mA cm−2 and 1 mAh cm−2, while the symmetric cell delivers an extended lifespan exceeding 1500 h at 1 mA cm−2 and 1 mAh cm−2. This work elucidates the electronic mechanism by which interfacial modification layers optimize sodium deposition behavior and SEI chemistry at the atomic scale, offering perspectives for the design of high-performance AFSMBs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used a high-entropy MXene interface to regulate sodium deposition, reducing nucleation overpotential and promoting an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase. The modified electrodes sustained over 400 hours in half-cells and more than 1,500 hours in symmetric cells, indicating a potentially consequential route to more durable anode-free sodium batteries.

articles.title_original: Electrostatic control of Li+ density and transport rate in double-gated van der Waals devices
articles.title_en: Double-gated van der Waals devices independently control Li+ density and transport
articles.excerpt_original: Ion transport in crystalline hosts is controlled by an applied potential that simultaneously sets ionic distribution and transport rate, restricting operation to a one-dimensional control space. Here we show that the transport rate of Li+ ions in double-gated van der Waals devices can be modulated while the system occupies fixed ionic-density states. We measure the ionic current along the van der Waals interfaces between hexagonal boron nitride and graphene or MoS2 while simultaneously monitoring the in-plane electronic response. The ionic current exhibits pronounced hysteresis, with plateaus marking discrete ionic-density states balanced by electronic charge, while an independently tuneable electrochemical-potential drop controls the ionic transport rate. The devices sustain over 1,000 switching cycles and function as hybrid ionic-electronic transistors capable of logic operations and memory retention, with ON/OFF ratios exceeding two orders of magnitude. This work demonstrates a two-dimensional control space for ions intercalated in layered materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate electrostatic control of lithium-ion density and transport rate in interfaces involving graphene and hexagonal boron nitride. The devices operate as hybrid ionic-electronic transistors, supporting more than 1,000 switching cycles, logic operations, and memory retention with ON/OFF ratios above 100×.

articles.title_original: End-to-end physics-based modeling of laser-activated color centers in silicon
articles.title_en: Physics-based laser activation of silicon color centers enables scalable quantum photonics
articles.excerpt_original: Color centers are among the most promising candidates for quantum information processing. Central requirements for their practical applications include controlled and efficient local activation in nanophotonic devices and identical spectral features. However, producing color centers in a controlled and reliable way is inherently challenging due to the lack of comprehensive theoretical insights into their formation and the difficulty of streamlining the generation process for rapid in-situ optimization. Here, we show an end-to-end first-principles model that captures the underlying formation process of color centers. Emitters are activated through laser annealing, which allows for in-situ creation and model-based control. Our model enables estimation of the emitters’ inhomogeneous broadening down to ~ 16GHz in bare silicon, translating into creation of emitters with highly similar spectral properties. We demonstrate successful laser writing in photonic crystal cavities. These results lay the foundation for deterministic and large-scale integration of color centers within quantum photonic platforms. Color centers in silicon can act as quantum light sources, but placing them reliably in photonic devices remains challenging. The authors show that laser annealing guided by a physics-based digital twin can locally create G centers with closely matched emission and write them into optical cavities.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an end-to-end first-principles model that guides laser annealing to create G centers in silicon with closely matched spectral properties. The approach enabled laser writing in photonic crystal cavities, supporting deterministic integration of quantum light sources into photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Nanoscale 2D field-effect transistors
articles.title_en: Review Examines Nanoscale Graphene and 2D Field-Effect Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: This chapter presents an in-depth examination of nanoscale field-effect transistors (FETs) based on two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors and carbon nanotubes (CNTs), highlighting their potential to extend device scaling beyond the limits of conventional silicon technologies. Beginning with the fundamental challenges of bulk and ultra-thin-body silicon transistors, this chapter introduces key classes of emerging channel materials including transition metal dichalcogenides, graphene, and CNTs. Also, analyzes how their atomically thin or one-dimensional geometries offer superior electrostatic integrity, reduced scattering, and improved short-channel behavior. Detailed discussions of device physics cover electrostatics, gate control, contact engineering, and carrier transport, supported by analytical, compact, and drift-diffusion/ballistic modeling approaches suitable for both device benchmarking and Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-level circuit simulations. This chapter further evaluates reliability concerns such as low-frequency noise, bias-induced degradation, and long-term stability, which are critical for the practical deployment of these technologies. Finally, it surveys emerging applications, including flexible electronics, neuromorphic architectures, biosensing, Radio Frequency (RF) systems, and energy-efficient logic which is followed by key challenges in material quality, variability, contact design, and modeling standardization. Collectively, this chapter provides a comprehensive foundation for advancing 2D- and CNT-based FETs toward next-generation nanoelectronic platforms.

articles.title_original: Elucidating the Impact of Bi 3+ Lone Pair on the Optical and Electronic Properties of Phosphonium‐Based Halide Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Phosphonium Halide Semiconductors Enable Wearable PFAS and PCB Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Hybrid metal halide semiconductors exhibit intriguing photophysical properties that are attributed to strong electron‐phonon coupling mediated by lattice deformations. Although extensive research has established a relatively clear picture of the effects of both intra‐octahedral and inter‐octahedral distortions on the optical and electronic behavior of 3D and 2D metal halide materials, there is still a lack of distortion descriptors to quantify octahedral distortions in edge‐sharing 0D dimers (oligomers). Here, we provide new structure distortion descriptors to accurately quantify the off‐centering of the metal cation from the geometric center of the octahedron and the twist angle between face‐sharing octahedra. As a testing platform, we synthesized two new 0D metal halides based on [Bi 2 I 9 ] 3− dimers using phosphonium organic cations, with general formula (L) 3 Bi 2 I 9 (L = butyl(trimethyl)phosphonium bromide (P5‐P), benzyl(triethyl)phosphonium bromide (P3‐P)). We correlated the inter‐octahedral twisting within the metal halide dimers with their photoluminescence at RT and 80 K, while their inherent water stability enabled the evaluation of their redox and sensing properties toward persistent organic pollutants. The assembly of flexible, wearable electrodes demonstrated the simultaneous determination of per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), underscoring their promise for portable field applications.

articles.title_original: Linker Engineering of Copper‐Based 2D Conductive Metal–Organic Frameworks for Modular Photo‐Mediated Properties and Multimodal Antibacterial Effects

articles.excerpt_original: Photoactive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have gained increasing attention in advanced photocatalysis and phototherapeutic applications. However, these MOFs suffer from insufficient structural tunability, which originates from the use of photoactive precursors with limited light absorption ranges or the incorporation of inorganic semiconductors to enhance light-harvesting performance. Therefore, the fabrication of intrinsic semiconducting MOFs with broadband light absorption and tunable photophysical properties represents a crucial endeavor for advancing photo-based technologies. Herein, we report a series of antibacterial agents derived from two-dimensional conductive metal-organic frameworks (2D c-MOFs) via linker engineering, employing commercially available linkers with distinct aromatic cores, namely tetrahydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone (THQ) and hexahydroxytriphenylene (HHTP). All three materials display broadband light-harvesting and good photothermal conversion capacity, and further exhibit light-enhanced and structural-dependent antibacterial activity. Mechanistic studies reveal that their measurable differences in antibacterial efficacy can be ascribed to linker-mediated variations in structural porosity, stability, and electronic delocalization that govern their photoelectronic properties and photocatalytic pathways. These 2D c-MOFs offer a materials paradigm and mechanistic basis for tailoring photo-mediated properties and multimodal antibacterial effects, and provide valuable insights for advanced photocatalysis and phototherapeutic applications.

articles.title_original: Low energy electron beam doping on graphene with enhanced carrier mobility
articles.title_en: Electron-Beam Doping Enhances Graphene Mobility and Enables Local Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In this study, we investigated low-energy electron-beam (e-beam) doping in graphene to achieve both effective n-type doping and enhanced carrier mobility. E-beam irradiation modifies graphene through surface cleaning and substrate charging, resulting in a pronounced shift of the Dirac point and improved carrier mobility; this behavior was corroborated by photocurrent polarity inversion at the metal contacts observed using scanning photocurrent microscopy (SPCM). In particular, electron–hole puddles near the charge neutrality point were visualized by SPCM, providing insight into the doping mechanism. We further identified optimized e-beam irradiation conditions that simultaneously enabled strong n-type doping and enhanced carrier mobility. Furthermore, by exploiting the high spatial resolution of e-beam lithography, we successfully fabricated local junction structures, including p–n and n–p–n junctions, within a single graphene channel without physical etching. The spatially modulated doping profiles were confirmed by the appearance of double Dirac peaks in electrical measurements together with SPCM mapping.

articles.title_original: Chiral Phonons and Giant Anisotropic Photoresponse in Quasi-1D van der Waals Semiconductor ZrSnS3
articles.title_en: ZrSnS3 Nanowires Show Chiral Phonons and Anisotropic Photoresponse
articles.excerpt_original: Low-dimensional van der Waals semiconductors with reduced symmetry provide a unique platform for exploring anisotropic physical properties. The quasi-one-dimensional family MXQ$_3$ (M = Hf, Zr; X = Sn; Q = S, Se) exhibits notable structural anisotropy, where zigzag atomic chains influence optical phenomena such as birefringence. This study investigates anisotropic lattice dynamics in ZrSnS$_3$ using angle- and polarization-dependent Raman spectroscopy. Temperature-dependent measurements reveal anharmonic phonon behavior, indicating strong phonon-phonon coupling. Density functional theory calculations show good agreement with the experimentally observed Raman spectra, validating the microscopic description of the lattice dynamics. We also observe a helicity-dependent intensity and a reversal in phonon intensity between lower- and higher-frequency modes under circularly polarized light, which is characteristic of chiral phonons governed by the polarization of the Zr/Sn chains. Our first-principles analysis further shows that angular-momentum-like phonon textures can emerge away from the $Γ$-point near mode-hybridization and avoided-crossing regions, providing microscopic insight into the observed helicity-dependent Raman signatures. Furthermore, we fabricate an optoelectronic device from a thin ZrSnS$_3$ nanowire, demonstrating a photoresponsivity of 50~mA/W under 520~nm laser excitation (1~mW/cm$^2$). The device exhibits a pronounced, power-scalable anisotropic photoresponse with a clear preferred polarization direction. These results highlight the coupling mechanisms between polarization, lattice vibrations, and charge carriers in ZrSnS$_3$, establishing it as a promising material for polarization-sensitive optoelectronics and directional quantum transport.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed helicity-dependent chiral phonon signatures in quasi-one-dimensional ZrSnS3 using polarization- and angle-resolved Raman spectroscopy. articles.excerpt_original: The exponential growth of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), which already accounts for ~10% of global electricity consumption, demands ultra-low-power semiconductors and has the potential to align with decarbonization goals and sustainability targets. This study optimizes Hafnium Zirconium oxide (Hf₀.₅Zr₀.₅O₂)-based ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) using 2D TCAD simulations of a metal-ferroelectric-insulator-semiconductor (MFIS) structure. The optimized device exhibits steep-subthreshold switching and low-voltage operation, indicating the potential for an ideal device-level dynamic power reduction of up to 75% through supply-voltage scaling, while the non-volatile ferroelectric state enables near-zero standby power at the memory-device level. Under the representative operating assumptions adopted in this study, these device-level improvements suggest the potential for reduced operational energy consumption in data-center memory workloads. Consequently, the proposed HZO-based FeFET architecture may contribute to lower ICT-related carbon emissions, although the reported sustainability benefits should be interpreted as scenario-based analytical estimates rather than deployment-specific predictions.
